Present: M/s. Junaid Anwar Khan, Hafiz Iftikhar Khan and
Sabtain Nisar Khan, Advocates for petitioners.,
M/s. Sajid-ur-Rehman Khan, Addl: AG for official
M/s. Waqar Ahmed Khan, Ms. Shabnam Nawaz and
Kiran Ayub Tanoli, Advocates for private respondents
J U D G M E N T
body: SYED MUDASSER AMEER, J. – Through this consolidated judgment, the above writ petitions and the connected contempt petition are being decided together. They arise from the recruitment process initiated for the appointment of Patwaris (BPS-09) in District Mansehra against twenty-one advertised posts. The dispute concerns the authority competent to conduct the initial screening test, the effect of the Government’s recruitment policy, and the legality of two separate tests held for the same vacancies.

2. The Deputy Commissioner, Mansehra, advertised twentyone posts of Patwari (BPS-09) through advertisements published in the daily newspapers Mashriq and Shamal on 22.08.2024. Candidates applied and, after scrutiny, a departmental written test was conducted on 21.09.2025. Its result was declared on the same day. The petitioners in Writ Petition No. 1200-A of 2025 claim to have qualified that test and seek completion of the remaining recruitment process, including their interviews and consideration for appointment.

3. Before appointments could be made, the Deputy Director (Administration) of the Educational Testing and Evaluation Agency, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (ETEA), addressed letter No. ETEA/2-3/Gen-Misc/9058-59 dated 22.09.2025 to the Deputy Commissioner, Mansehra. The letter referred to the Government notification dated 27.04.2021, issued in pursuance of section 4(1)(d) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Educational Testing and Evaluation Agency Ordinance, 2001. It pointed out that the conduct of screening tests for recruitment to posts in Government departments and other public bodies had been assigned to ETEA. It further stated that the recruitment in question had not been referred to ETEA and that no request had been received for a No Objection Certificate to use another testing arrangement.

4. Upon receipt of that communication, the Deputy Commissioner stopped the departmental recruitment process. By letter No. 5120-24/DK dated 25.09.2025, his office requested ETEA to conduct a test for the same candidates on a priority basis. ETEA accordingly conducted a screening test on 12.10.2025 and transmitted the result to the appointing authority. A second group of candidates, including the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 1341-A of 2025, relies upon that result and seeks continuation of the recruitment process on its basis.

5. Most of the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 1200-A of 2025 did not appear in the ETEA test. They maintain that they had already participated in the departmental test, had qualified it, and were awaiting interviews. They further contend that their writ petition was pending before this Court and that they reasonably expected the recruitment process commenced through the official advertisement to be taken to its lawful conclusion. They therefore challenge the decision to abandon the departmental test and subject the candidates to a second examination.

6. In Writ Petition No. 1403-A of 2025, Noman Shah and others challenge the ETEA communication, the subsequent test and its result. They seek continuation of the original departmental process. In Writ Petition No. 1341-A of 2025, Mohsin Ali and others question the departmental test and seek to proceed on the basis of the ETEA test. Thus, the candidates who succeeded in the two examinations assert competing claims to consideration against the same vacancies.

7. The Deputy Commissioner, in his comments, admits the advertisement, the conduct of the departmental test and declaration of its result. He maintains that the process was stopped after ETEA brought the Government notification to his notice. His office states that a request for a No Objection Certificate had been made to the Finance Department and that approval had been accorded for seventeen posts. It nevertheless requested ETEA to conduct a test for the same candidates. ETEA, for its part, maintains that the test held on 12.10.2025 was conducted fairly and in accordance with its rules, regulations and Standard Operating Procedures. It denies any mala fide, favouritism or discrimination.

8. The connected contempt petition alleges disobedience of the interim order dated 08.10.2025 passed in Writ Petition No. 1200-A of 2025. By that order, the respondents were permitted to continue the process strictly in accordance with law but were restrained from passing any final order. The Deputy Commissioner forwarded a copy of the order to ETEA on 10.10.2025. The test was held two days later. No appointment order has been brought to the notice of the Court.

9. Learned counsel for the petitioners supporting the departmental result submits that the Deputy Commissioner is the competent appointing authority for Patwaris. It is argued that the candidates applied pursuant to a public advertisement, appeared in the test arranged by the district administration, and qualified on merit. The authorities cannot, after having invited applications and declared the result, deny the successful candidates further consideration merely by relying upon a later communication from ETEA. The petitioners maintain that their legitimate expectation must be respected.

10. Learned counsel for the petitioners supporting the ETEA test submits that the Government had already assigned screening tests to ETEA under the notification dated 27.04.2021. The departmental test was therefore contrary to the applicable recruitment framework. It is contended that the subsequent test was the proper course, although the petitioners also seek scrutiny of the formalities adopted in conducting it.

11. The learned Additional Advocate General and learned counsel appearing for ETEA submit that the Government notification was binding upon the district administration. They contend that a departmental test could not lawfully be substituted for the assigned screening test without the required No Objection Certificate. ETEA further asserts that its test was conducted transparently and that the petitioners who did not appear in it cannot insist that its result be set aside.

12. Arguments have been heard and the record perused. The controversy cannot be resolved simply by preferring one result over the other. The Court must determine the lawful method of recruitment, whether either test complied with that method, and what relief can fairly be granted to candidates who participated in the competing exercises.

13. The starting point is the legal framework governing the appointment of Patwaris. Paragraph 3.6 of the Land Record Manual provides for maintenance of a list of Patwar-pass persons in each sub-division. It also makes clear that appointments are to be made strictly in accordance with the service rules and recruitment policy applicable at the relevant time. The list is intended to identify eligible candidates; it is not, by itself, a substitute for the prescribed selection process.

14. The recruitment framework was considered by a larger Bench of this Court in Ameer Taimoor and 7 others v. Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through Senior Member Board of Revenue and others (2016 PLC (C.S.) 106; 2015 CLC 1824). The Court held that appointment of Patwaris must conform to the Land Record Manual, the applicable service rules and the prevailing recruitment policy. It reiterated the established rule that where the law prescribes a method for doing an act, the act must be done in that manner and not otherwise. The judgment also recognized that the Government may revise the recruitment framework in accordance with law.

15. The method of recruitment was subsequently addressed through the amendment notified by the Revenue and Estate Department on 25.11.2016. The amended framework provides for initial appointment from among Patwar-passed candidates entered in the relevant register, on the basis of a test and interview conducted after advertisement of the posts. In Salah-ud-Din v. Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through Secretary Revenue and Estate and others (2023 PLC (C.S.) 408), this Court recognized the effect of the amended rules and held that appointment must be made in accordance with the service rules and recruitment policy applicable to the recruitment in question.

16. The same approach was adopted in Muhammad Yaqoob and another v. Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and others, Writ Petition No. 340-D of 2016 and connected petitions, decided on 27.11.2019. The Court explained that paragraph 3.6 of the Land Record Manual must be read with the governing service rules and recruitment policy. The mere fact that a candidate has passed the Patwar examination or has been entered in the Patwar candidates register does not confer an indefeasible right to appointment outside the prescribed process.

17. The next question is the statutory role of ETEA. Section 4(1)(d) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Educational Testing and Evaluation Agency Ordinance, 2001, empowers the Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, to assign additional functions to the Agency. Section 14 provides that the Ordinance shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force.

18. In exercise of the power conferred by section 4(1)(d), the Government issued the notification dated 27.04.2021, assigning to ETEA the conduct of screening tests for posts in Government departments, attached departments, Government organizations, and autonomous and semi-autonomous bodies in the Province. The notification also provides the mechanism for an alternative testing arrangement where ETEA declines or is unable to conduct a particular test. In such circumstances, a No Objection Certificate is to be issued by ETEA, with reasons recorded in writing, so that a suitable testing agency may be hired in accordance with the applicable procurement rules.

19. The notification must be read with the Government’s policy on merit and transparency in recruitment and the Standard Operating Procedures framed by ETEA. Under the policy, initial screening for regular and ad hoc positions in BPS-7 to BPS-14 is to be conducted through ETEA, subject to the specified exceptions. Those exceptions include posts of a purely specialized nature, positions involving manual or physical skills, genuine exigencies supported by cogent reasons, and cases in which ETEA is unable to conduct a test within the required schedule and the prescribed No Objection Certificate is obtained. The post of Patwari (BPS-09) does not fall, on the record before us, within any such exception.

20. The legal effect of the notification is important. It assigns the initial screening function to ETEA. It does not transfer the entire recruitment process or the power of appointment to the Agency. The requirements of the Patwari service rules concerning eligibility, entry in the Patwar candidates register, interview and final selection continue to apply. The Deputy Commissioner or other competent authority remains responsible for the remaining selection proceedings and appointment. ETEA is entrusted with the screening function so that the initial assessment is conducted through the prescribed agency in a standardized and transparent manner.

21. The provisions can therefore operate together. The Patwari service rules prescribe who may be considered and require selection through the prescribed test and interview after advertisement. The Government’s notification assigns the initial screening test to ETEA. There is no conflict between those requirements. The appointing authority must observe both. The overriding clause in section 14 gives effect to the Ordinance where a conflict with another law arises; it does not extinguish the service rules or confer upon ETEA a power of appointment that the rules have assigned to another authority.

22. The departmental test held on 21.09.2025 was conducted by the district administration itself. It was held after the Government notification had been issued, and there is no material to show that the recruitment had been referred to ETEA before the examination or that an appropriate No Objection Certificate had been obtained from ETEA to use an alternative testing arrangement. The Finance Department approval mentioned in the Deputy Commissioner’s letter does not, by itself, meet that requirement. Approval concerning the availability or sanction of posts is distinct from permission to depart from the prescribed testing arrangement.

23. The explanation that the notification came to the Deputy Commissioner’s attention only after ETEA’s letter dated 22.09.2025 does not alter the legal position. A public authority proposing to recruit civil servants must ascertain the applicable rules, notifications and policy before issuing an advertisement and conducting a test. Administrative oversight cannot authorize departure from a binding recruitment framework. Nor can the successful candidates’ performance in the departmental examination validate a process that was not conducted in accordance with the applicable arrangement.

24. This does not mean that the candidates who qualified the departmental test acted improperly. They responded to an official advertisement and participated in an examination arranged by the district administration. Their reliance on that process is understandable. It gives rise to a legitimate expectation that the authorities will treat them fairly and provide a lawful opportunity to compete. It does not, however, confer an indefeasible right to insist that a selection process contrary to the governing law must be completed.

25. The distinction between a right to appointment and an expectation of lawful treatment is well established. In Government of Punjab through Secretary (S&GAD) v. Zafar Maqbool Khan (2012 SCMR 686), the Supreme Court emphasized that eligibility must be assessed according to the governing service rules, the applicable advertisement and instructions backed by law. A candidate’s success in an examination does not permit the authority or the Court to disregard the governing legal requirements.

26. The principle was applied directly in Punjab Public Service Commission and others v. Husnain Abbas and others (2021 SCMR 1017). The Supreme Court held that no vested right to appointment accrued through an erroneous merit list prepared on the basis of an advertisement that violated the applicable Government policy and rules. The Court rejected the contention that legitimate expectation could prevail over the legal rights created by the valid policy and notifications. The principle applies here. The candidates who qualified the departmental test cannot claim appointment, or insist upon continuation of that test, merely because the result has been declared.

27. The principle of legitimate expectation nevertheless requires careful consideration. In Uzma Manzoor and others v. Vice-Chancellor, Khushal Khan Khattak University, Karak and others (2022 SCMR 690), the Supreme Court explained that such an expectation may arise from a promise, assurance, established practice or policy of a public authority. It is a means of ensuring fairness in administrative action. It does not, however, authorize a public authority to act contrary to law.

28. In District Education Officer (Female), Charsadda and others v. Sonia Begum and others (2023 SCMR 217), the Supreme Court considered the position of candidates who had been permitted to compete and had qualified but were later excluded on the basis of the documents they had submitted. The Court attached importance to the fact that the relevant scrutiny could have been carried out at an earlier stage. That decision protects candidates against arbitrary administrative treatment in a recruitment process which they were permitted to enter. It does not establish that a process which contravenes a binding requirement concerning the authority to conduct the screening test must be upheld merely because candidates have succeeded in it.

29. This Court’s decision in Israr Mehmood and others v. Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through Chief Secretary and another, Writ Petition No. 206-A of 2022, decided on 21.09.2023, also requires consideration. In that case, candidates had responded to a public advertisement which expressly identified an independent private testing service. They had appeared in the written and physical tests, had qualified, and their merit list had been forwarded to the department. The department then declined to proceed further, relying upon the fact that the tests had not been conducted by ETEA. In those circumstances, the Court held that the objection could not defeat the candidates’ legitimate expectation and directed that they be called for interview and that the process be completed according to law.

30. The present case is materially different. In Israr Mehmood, the examination had been conducted through an independent testing service expressly identified in the advertisement. The controversy concerned a single testing exercise, and the Court found no allegation of irregularity in the examination or the preparation of the merit list. Here, the initial test was conducted by the district administration itself, despite the notified assignment of screening tests to ETEA. More importantly, the authorities then arranged a second test for the same vacancies, producing two separate groups of candidates whose results cannot both be adopted as the basis of selection. The issue is not merely whether the first group should be allowed to proceed to interview. It is whether the recruitment can lawfully be completed on either of two inconsistent testing exercises.

31. The Supreme Court’s decision in Husnain Abbas also requires that legitimate expectation be balanced against the controlling legal framework. The candidates’ expectation in the present case is real, but it must be given effect in a manner consistent with the governing rules. It cannot validate the departmental test. At the same time, the candidates who did not appear in the later test should not be treated as having forfeited every opportunity to compete merely because they relied upon the earlier process while their challenge was pending before this Court.

32. The ETEA test cannot, however, be adopted automatically as the lawful result. ETEA was the appropriate agency to conduct the initial screening test, but the manner in which the second exercise was arranged raises separate procedural concerns. The Deputy Commissioner’s letter dated 25.09.2025 asked ETEA to conduct the test for the same candidates on a priority basis. ETEA’s comments state that it received the requisite data from the district administration and conducted the test in accordance with its rules and Standard Operating Procedures. The record, however, does not establish that the recruitment-specific arrangements were settled and documented in the manner required by those procedures.

33. ETEA’s Standard Operating Procedures, notified on 27.08.2021, contemplate a request from the client organization followed by consideration of the particular assignment and discussion of the arrangements. These include the mechanism for advertisement, receipt and scrutiny of applications, roll numbers, test dates and centers, the composition and qualifying criteria of the test, the declaration of results and any other conditions governing the exercise. The procedures further contemplate that the agreed arrangements be recorded in a memorandum of understanding or terms and conditions. The official recruitment policy also provides for advertisement of vacancies through ETEA at the expense of the recruiting entity.

34. Although the original advertisement had been published by the Deputy Commissioner, it preceded the later referral to ETEA and the first departmental test. The ETEA exercise was then arranged by a short communication requesting a test from the same candidates. The record does not establish that the manner of advertisement, the application process, the eligibility scrutiny, the qualifying criteria and the terms governing the second test had been settled in advance through the required recruitment-specific arrangements. Nor does the record sufficiently establish that the change from the original process to the ETEA process provided a common and fair opportunity to all eligible candidates. ETEA’s general assertion that the test was transparent does not answer these procedural concerns.

35. It is not necessary to hold that the absence of a fresh ETEA advertisement, in every case, would invalidate a screening test. ETEA’s own procedures contemplate that, depending upon the agreed arrangement, advertisement and receipt of applications may be handled either by ETEA or by the recruiting organization. The defect here lies in the absence of a demonstrated, settled and transparent arrangement governing the second exercise, coupled with the unequal position in which candidates were placed after the first test had already been held and its result declared. A fresh process will remove that uncertainty and ensure that all eligible candidates compete under the same announced conditions.

36. The matter therefore cannot be resolved by retaining the departmental result and directing interviews for those who passed it. That would give effect to a test conducted contrary to the notified screening arrangement. Nor can the ETEA result simply be adopted, because the second exercise was arranged after the original process had been halted and was not shown to have complied with all the procedural requirements governing a transparent recruitment exercise. The two results cannot be reconciled by selecting one group over the other. Both tests must be set aside and the process restarted.

37. This conclusion does not visit the fault of the authorities upon the candidates. Neither group can claim an indefeasible right to appointment merely because its members passed one of the examinations. The candidates have a right to fair and lawful consideration. That right is best protected by a fresh process, with a single testing arrangement, an adequate and publicized opportunity to apply, settled criteria and equal treatment. All candidates who satisfy the eligibility requirements, including those who applied under the original advertisement and those who appeared in either of the previous tests, shall be entitled to compete in the fresh process. No preference or credit shall accrue merely from participation in, or success in, either of the earlier tests.

38. Before the fresh process is advertised, the official respondents shall also clarify the number of posts duly sanctioned and vacant. The Deputy Commissioner’s letter dated 25.09.2025 refers to approval from the Finance Department for seventeen posts, whereas the original advertisement invited applications against twenty-one posts. The record does not adequately explain this difference. Recruitment must be confined to duly sanctioned and available vacancies. The fresh process may cover all twenty-one posts if the competent authorities verify that all are sanctioned and vacant; otherwise, it shall be confined to the number lawfully available, and the position shall be clearly stated in the advertisement.

39. The question of age requires separate consideration. The first test was conducted by the Deputy Commissioner on 21.09.2025. Candidates who were within the prescribed age limit on that date had entered the recruitment process and participated in the test arranged by the official respondents. The process was subsequently halted and both testing exercises now require repetition because the authorities failed to follow a coherent and lawful recruitment procedure. Some candidates may, in the meantime, have crossed the prescribed upper age limit. They cannot fairly be made to suffer this additional consequence for a delay attributable to the very authorities responsible for conducting the recruitment. Their legitimate expectation may not confer a vested right to appointment, nor can it validate either of the disputed tests. It does, however, entitle them to protection against loss of eligibility caused solely by the delay and errors of the official respondents. Accordingly, candidates who were within the prescribed age limit on 21.09.2025 shall be permitted to participate in the fresh recruitment process for the posts in question, notwithstanding that they may have since become overage. This protection is confined to the present recruitment and shall not be treated as a general relaxation of the prescribed age limit. It shall neither dispense with any other eligibility requirement nor confer any preference in the selection process. The principle recognized in Muhammad Aamir Khan v. Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and others (2019 SCMR 1021), concerning the prohibition against relaxation of age in the face of an express statutory restriction, does not require candidates to bear the adverse consequences of an administrative failure in circumstances where the Court is preserving their eligibility as it stood when the first test was conducted. The object is not to confer an additional benefit, but to prevent an existing opportunity from being lost through no fault of the candidates.

40. No finding is required upon the allegations of political interference, manipulation, favouritism or other misconduct. The present decision rests upon the applicable recruitment framework and the procedural defects in the two testing exercises. Nothing in this judgment shall be understood as an adverse finding regarding the integrity, competence or suitability of any candidate. Their comparative merit has not been adjudicated.

41. The contempt petition arises from the interim order dated 08.10.2025, which permitted the respondents to continue the process strictly in accordance with law but restrained them from passing a final order. The ETEA test was conducted on 12.10.2025, after the order had been forwarded to the Agency. The testing exercise was an intermediate step; no final appointment order was passed. In the circumstances, and in view of the directions now being issued for a fresh process, it is unnecessary to record any finding of willful disobedience. The substantive controversy underlying the contempt petition has been resolved, and the contempt petition has become infructuous.

42. For the foregoing reasons, Writ Petition No. 1200-A of 2025, Writ Petition No. 1341-A of 2025 and Writ Petition No. 1403-A of 2025 are disposed of in the following terms: (i) The departmental test conducted by the Deputy Commissioner, Mansehra, on 21.09.2025, its result, and all consequential proceedings founded upon that test are set aside.
(ii) The screening test conducted by ETEA on 12.10.2025, its result, and all consequential proceedings founded upon that test are also set aside.

(iii) The official respondents shall initiate a fresh recruitment process through ETEA for the duly sanctioned and vacant Patwari posts advertised on 22.08.2024, subject to verification of the number of posts lawfully available. If all twenty-one posts are duly sanctioned and vacant, the fresh process shall cover all twenty-one posts. If fewer posts are sanctioned and vacant, recruitment shall be restricted to that number unless the requisite sanction for the remaining posts is obtained.

(iv) Before the fresh advertisement is issued, the recruiting authority and ETEA shall settle and document the terms governing the recruitment, including the eligibility requirements, application procedure, fee, scrutiny of applications, testing arrangements, qualifying criteria and result procedure. A fresh and adequate public advertisement shall be issued through ETEA in accordance with the applicable Government recruitment policy and ETEA’s Standard Operating Procedures.

(v) ETEA shall conduct the initial screening test in accordance with the applicable notification, policy and prescribed procedure. The remaining selection proceedings, including scrutiny of eligibility, interview and final assessment, shall be undertaken by the competent appointing authority in accordance with the applicable Patwari service rules. ETEA shall not be treated as the appointing authority.

(vi) All otherwise eligible candidates, including those who applied under the original advertisement and those who participated in either of the earlier tests, shall be permitted to compete in the fresh process. No preference or credit shall be given merely because a candidate participated in, or qualified, either of the earlier tests. (vii) Candidates who applied against the advertisement dated 22.08.2024 and were within the prescribed age limit on 21.09.2025, the date of the first test conducted by the Deputy Commissioner, shall be permitted to participate in the fresh recruitment process, even if they have since crossed the prescribed upper age limit. The competent authority shall verify their dates of birth and eligibility as on the said date. This protection shall be confined to the twenty-one posts in question and shall not dispense with any other eligibility requirement or confer any preference in merit.

(viii) The official respondents shall coordinate with one another to complete the fresh recruitment process expeditiously and strictly in accordance with law. No appointment shall be made against a post that is not duly sanctioned and vacant.

43. Contempt of Court Petition No. 107-A of 2025 is disposed of as having become infructuous, without recording a finding of wilful disobedience. Any interim orders operating in the connected matters shall stand discharged. The parties shall bear their own costs. A copy of this judgment shall be placed on the files of all connected cases.
Announced.

Recruitment; Departmental test; Non-compliance with prescribed procedure; Vested right. A public authority proposing to recruit civil servants must ascertain the applicable rules, notifications and policy before issuing an advertisement and conducting a test. Administrative oversight cannot authorise departure from a binding recruitment framework. Nor can the successful candidates’ performance in the departmental examination validate a process that was not conducted in accordance with the applicable arrangement. Candidates who qualified the departmental test cannot claim appointment, or insist upon continuation of that test, merely because the result has been declared. (Punjab Public Service Commission and others v. Husnain Abbas and others, 2021 SCMR 1017). (Paras 23-26) Legitimate expectation; Public recruitment; Competing tests; Fair opportunity. The candidates who qualified the departmental test cannot claim an indefeasible right to appointment. Their participation and success cannot, by themselves, require continuation of a process without regard to the governing recruitment framework. At the same time, the candidates who did not appear in the later test should not be treated as having forfeited every opportunity to compete merely because they relied upon the earlier process while their challenge was pending before this Court. All candidates who satisfy the eligibility requirements shall be entitled to compete in the fresh process. No preference or credit shall accrue merely from participation in, or success in, either of the earlier tests. (Paras 24, 31, 37) Recruitment; Age limit; Administrative delay; Legitimate expectation. Candidates who were within the prescribed age limit on 21.09.2025 shall be permitted to participate in the fresh recruitment process for the posts in question, notwithstanding that they may have since become overage. Their legitimate expectation may not confer a vested right to appointment, nor can it validate either of the disputed tests. It does, however, entitle them to protection against loss of eligibility caused solely by the delay and errors of the official respondents. This protection shall be confined to the present recruitment and shall not be treated as a general relaxation of the prescribed age limit. It shall neither dispense with any other eligibility requirement nor confer any preference in the selection process. (Para 39) Held: Both the departmental test dated 21.09.2025 and the ETEA test dated 12.10.2025, along with their respective results and consequential proceedings, set aside. Fresh recruitment directed through ETEA for the duly sanctioned and vacant posts, following a fresh advertisement and compliance with the applicable service rules, Government policy and prescribed procedure. Candidates who were within the prescribed age limit on the date of the first test protected against becoming overage as a consequence of administrative delay. (Paras 36-42)
